Q: How to distribute a Ruby script via Homebrew A:

It's a technique used by someone on the Internet. Basically, do something like this

#!/usr/bin/env ruby
DBMGR_HOME = File.expand_path('../..', __FILE__)
$LOAD_PATH.unshift(File.join(DBMGR_HOME, 'lib'))
require 'dbmgr'

And the recipe can be like this:

https://github.com/callahanrts/homebrew-dbmgr/blob/master/dbmgr.rb

Q: How to implement an efficient Human-in-the-loop workflow for AI-driven ERP risk analysis? A:

A practical approach is to store human feedback as labeled events and periodically update the model using mini-batch or incremental learning (e.g., partial_fit). To avoid drift, retrain a baseline model on a schedule. For interpretability, libraries like SHAP or LIME can visualize why risks were flagged, enabling informed human review in a UI such as Streamlit.

Q: How can an embedded database support PostgreSQL syntax without running a PostgreSQL server? A:

What are the common approaches used by embedded databases to support PostgreSQL-compatible syntax?

The common approach is to run PostgreSQL. For example Zonky Embedded PostgreSQL uses standard PostgreSQL binaries, it just runs a short-lived instance from the client instead of configuring a daemon service.

This is a fork of OpenTable Embedded PostgreSQL which now runs PostgreSQL in a Docker container.

I understand this is not what you want to do.

Are there open-source projects or references for implementing a PostgreSQL-like query planner in a lightweight engine?

There are packages to implement a PostgreSQL-compatible query parser, for example pganalyze/libpg_query.

Parsing the query to validate the syntax and allow you to inspect the AST (abstract syntax tree) is the first step of handling a query, but this does not execute the query or return any results.

Implementing a whole query engine to execute queries is a different task. You have to implement storage, concurrency, security, and so on. If you intend pglite to be embedded, at least you don't have to implement networking.

Is it realistic to support a meaningful subset of PostgreSQL features without implementing the full PostgreSQL architecture?

If you are the only user of pglite, then you can implement the subset of features you will need in your project.

But if you expect other people to use pglite, very soon you will get requests for features of PostgreSQL you didn't think were important, but are needed for their project.

For example, do you intend to implement user-defined functions, triggers, procedures, and rules? If not, how will you respond to users who say they want to use pglite to test their application, but they have developed hundreds of such stored routines?

How about system catalogs and system views?

How about the thousands of builtin functions of PostgreSQL? Not just for JSON, but array functions, set returning functions, full text search, system information...

How about the many popular extensions to PostgreSQL, like PostGIS, pgcrypto, pg_stat_statements, pgvector, tablefunc, and many others. You may even be requested to implement extensions that are deprecated, because some users still rely on those extensions.

Another thing you need to decide is which version of PostgreSQL does pglite support? New features are added in each version, as well as more subtle changes to the behavior of, for instance, the query planner.

If your embedded solution emulates PostgreSQL syntax and behavior, you will have to track the PostgreSQL project continually and update your pglite project to match. Alternatively, declare that pglite is compatible only with PostgreSQL 18.1 and leave that fixed for all time.

The bottom line is that it may be possible to implement a subset of PostgreSQL functionality. This may cover 90% of what any user needs. But if every user only gets 90% of what they need, that means none the users get all of what they need.
